Print, Summarise and Tidy an LSA Fit

Source: R/lsa.R, R/methods-lsa.R
lsa-methods.Rd

Methods for the objects returned by lsa(). print() gives a compact model overview: engine, sizes, the tablewise independence test, the strongest over-represented transitions, and the initial-state distribution. summary() prints that overview followed by the node activity and the observed, expected, probability and residual matrices, and returns a one-row tidy overview. as.data.frame() returns the full edge table, including the integer ids and cograph_network protocol columns that transitions() leaves out. nobs() is the number of transitions the model was fitted to.

Usage

# S3 method for class 'lsa_group'
print(x, ...)

# S3 method for class 'lsa'
print(x, ...)

# S3 method for class 'lsa'
summary(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'lsa'
as.data.frame(x, row.names = NULL, optional = FALSE, ...)

# S3 method for class 'lsa_group'
as.data.frame(x, row.names = NULL, optional = FALSE, ...)

# S3 method for class 'lsa_group'
summary(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'lsa'
nobs(object, ...)

Arguments

x, object

An lsa fit from lsa(), or (for the lsa_group methods) a grouped fit from lsa(..., group = ).

...

Ignored.

row.names

Optional row names for the returned data frame (as.data.frame.lsa() only); ignored by the grouped method.

optional

Ignored; present for consistency with the generic.

Value

  • print() returns x invisibly.

  • summary.lsa() prints the extended view and returns, invisibly, a one-row data.frame with columns engine, lag, n_states, n_sequences, n_events, n_transitions, n_significant, alpha, lrx2, lrx2_df, lrx2_p, x2, x2_df, x2_p (NA where the engine computed no tablewise test or the input was a transition matrix).

  • summary.lsa_group() returns that frame visibly with one row per group and a leading group column; it prints nothing else.

  • as.data.frame.lsa() returns a data.frame with one row per from -> to cell: integer from/to ids, from_label, to_label, the statistic columns of transitions(), and the protocol columns edge and weight. as.data.frame.lsa_group() stacks these with a leading group column.

  • nobs() returns a single number, the total transition count.

Details

For reading results, prefer the verbs: transitions() for the per-transition table, nodes(), tests() and initial() for the other parts of the fit.

See also

lsa(), transitions()

Examples

fit <- lsa(engagement)
print(fit)
#> Lag Sequential Analysis  -  classical  (lag 1, directed)
#>   3 states | 1734 transitions | 1870 events | 136 sequences
#>   states: Active, Average, Disengaged
#>   independence: G² = 618.3, df = 4, p <2e-16
#> 
#>   Significant transitions (p < 0.05): 7 of 9
#>   strongest over-represented (of 3):
#>     Active -> Active          z =  +21.7  ***
#>     Disengaged -> Disengaged  z =  +15.4  ***
#>     Average -> Average        z =  +12.5  ***
#> 
#>   Initial states:
#>     Active     0.382  ████████████████████████
#>     Average    0.368  ███████████████████████
#>     Disengaged 0.250  ████████████████
summary(fit)

gfit <- lsa(group_regulation_long, actor = "Actor", action = "Action",
            time = "Time", group = "Achiever")
gfit

summary(gfit)
